definition:
The return of Christ is the church's confession that the same Jesus who was crucified, raised, and taken up into heaven will come again, in person, in his body, and in public glory, to raise the dead, judge the world, and bring God's kingdom to its completion in a renewed creation. It is not a way of speaking about Christ coming to each believer at death, or coming by his Spirit at Pentecost, or coming into history whenever justice advances, though the New Testament speaks of his presence in all those ways. It is a future event with a before and an after. The angels at the ascension put it in one sentence: “This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). Every ancient creed confesses it, and Christians who disagree sharply about the order of the last events agree on this.

The New Testament has three main words for it. Parousia means ‘presence’ or ‘arrival’; in the Greek-speaking world it was used for the arrival of a ruler or high official at a city, and Paul also uses it for the ordinary arrival of friends (1 Corinthians 16:17; 2 Corinthians 7:6), so the word does not carry a technical meaning by itself. Applied to Jesus (Matthew 24:27; 1 Thessalonians 4:15; James 5:8; 1 John 2:28), it means his royal arrival. Epiphaneia means ‘appearing’ or ‘manifestation’, used of both his first coming (2 Timothy 1:10) and his second (Titus 2:13), which ties the two together as one saving work in two acts. Apokalypsis means ‘unveiling’ or ‘revelation’ (1 Corinthians 1:7; 2 Thessalonians 1:7): the one who reigns now, hidden, will be seen. Behind all three stands the Old Testament phrase ‘the Day of the LORD’ (yom YHWH), which the apostles rename ‘the day of Christ’ (Philippians 1:6). The phrase ‘second coming’ is not itself in the New Testament, but Hebrews comes close when it says that Christ “will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him” (Hebrews 9:28).
ot:
The Old Testament does not speak of a second coming, because it has not yet seen the first. What it hopes for is larger and stranger: that God himself will come. The pattern is set at Sinai, where the LORD descends in fire and cloud to meet his people (Exodus 19), and the Psalms turn it into a song about the future. “He is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness” (Psalm 96:13). In Psalm 96 and Psalm 98 the trees and the sea rejoice at his coming, because his judging means the setting right of a world gone wrong. In exile Isaiah hears a voice cry “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness” (Isaiah 40:3) and a herald told to say to the towns of Judah, “Here is your God!” (Isaiah 40:9). Later a prophet prays, “If only You would rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). The Gospels will hear Isaiah 40 fulfilled in John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus, which is one of the ways the New Testament identifies Jesus' coming with the coming of Israel's God.

The prophets gave this hope a name, the Day of the LORD, and they warned that it would not flatter Israel. Amos, preaching in the eighth century BC, told those who longed for it, “Woe to you who long for the Day of the LORD! What will the Day of the LORD be for you? It will be darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18). Isaiah says the day will come “against all the proud and lofty” (Isaiah 2:12), Zephaniah calls it “a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress” (Zephaniah 1:15), and Joel pictures the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood before it arrives (Joel 2:31). Malachi, among the last of the prophets, promises that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” and then asks, “But who can endure the day of His coming?” (Malachi 3:1-2). He also promises that Elijah will be sent “before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). The prophets saw one great day of God's arrival, with salvation and judgment bound together in it. They did not separate it into stages. The New Testament will find that the one day comes in two acts, and that the first act brought mostly mercy.

Two visions give the hope a human face. In Daniel 7, written against the background of the empires that crushed Israel, a court sits in heaven, and Daniel sees “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” who approaches the Ancient of Days and receives “dominion, glory, and kingship” and a kingdom “that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13-14). In the vision this figure comes to God's throne rather than down to earth; his coming is his vindication and enthronement after the beasts have raged. The chapter also links him to “the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:27), the suffering people who share his reign. Jesus will take “Son of Man” as his favorite name for himself. Zechariah 14 pictures the LORD going out to fight for Jerusalem: “On that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4), “and all the holy ones with Him” (Zechariah 14:5), until “the LORD will become King over all the earth” (Zechariah 14:9). Two chapters earlier the people “will look on Me, the One they have pierced” and mourn (Zechariah 12:10), a line John applies both to the crucifixion (John 19:37) and to the return (Revelation 1:7). Alongside these stands Psalm 110:1, where David's Lord is told to sit at God's right hand “until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet”, among the Old Testament verses the New Testament quotes and echoes most often, which sets up the long session in heaven that the return brings to an end.
nt:
Jesus speaks of his return most often through the title Son of Man, drawn from Daniel 7. He warns that whoever is ashamed of him will find the Son of Man ashamed of him “when He comes in His Father's glory” (Mark 8:38), and in the long speech on the Mount of Olives (Mark 13; Matthew 24 and 25; Luke 21) he foretells the temple's destruction, wars, persecution, and false messiahs, and then “they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory” to gather his elect (Mark 13:26-27). At his trial he tells the high priest, “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62), joining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7 in one sentence. His coming will be as public as lightning across the sky (Matthew 24:27; Luke 17:24), as sudden as the flood in Noah's day (Matthew 24:37-39), and as unexpected as a thief (Matthew 24:43). The time is hidden: “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36). So the parables that follow, the servant left in charge, the ten virgins, the talents, all teach one thing: keep watch by being faithful at the task you were given. In John's Gospel the promise is personal: “I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am” (John 14:3).

One sentence in the speech has troubled readers for a long time: “this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened” (Mark 13:30). Albert Schweitzer argued in 1906 that Jesus expected the end within his hearers' lifetime and was mistaken. Many interpreters answer that ‘all these things’ refers to the events leading up to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which did happen within a generation, while the day and hour of the final coming in the next verses are left unknown. R. T. France and N. T. Wright go further and read the Son of Man's coming in Mark 13:26 itself as his vindication, in Daniel's sense, displayed in the judgment on the temple, with the final return taught elsewhere. Others read ‘generation’ as ‘this kind of people’. What the text will not allow is date-setting, since Jesus in the same breath says the hour is hidden.

The apostles made the return the horizon of the whole Christian life. At the ascension the angels promise that Jesus will return “in the same way” (Acts 1:11), and Peter preaches that heaven must receive him “until the time comes for the restoration of all things” (Acts 3:21). Paul's first letters answer anxious questions. To believers grieving their dead he writes that “the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and the living will be caught up “to meet the Lord in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The word for meeting, apantēsis, was used for citizens going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him back to their city (Acts 28:15 uses it for the believers who came out from Rome to meet Paul); many read the scene that way, while others note the word itself does not settle what happens after the meeting. To Christians told the day had already come, he says it will not come before a great rebellion and the revelation of ‘the man of lawlessness’, whom the Lord will destroy “by the majesty of His arrival” (2 Thessalonians 2:3-8). The return brings the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:23, 51-52; Philippians 3:20-21) and the public appearing of the hidden life believers already have in Christ (Colossians 3:4). Paul's letters also preserve an Aramaic prayer from the first Jewish believers, marana tha, ‘Our Lord, come’ (1 Corinthians 16:22), and he tells the Corinthians that every Lord's Supper proclaims the Lord's death “until He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Titus calls the return “the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13), and most grammarians read that phrase as naming Jesus both God and Savior.

The later letters address delay. James urges patience like a farmer waiting for rain (James 5:7-8). 2 Peter answers scoffers who ask “Where is the promise of His coming?” (2 Peter 3:4) by saying that God does not count time as we do and that his patience is mercy, “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9); the day will still come like a thief, bringing “a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). John writes that “when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2), and draws the moral straight away: the one who has this hope purifies himself. Revelation opens with “Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him” (Revelation 1:7), pictures the rider called Faithful and True whose name is The Word of God (Revelation 19:11-16), and closes the Bible with the promise and the prayer together: “Yes, I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). How Revelation 19 and 20 fit together, and where the thousand years of Revelation 20 belong, is the question on which Christians divide; the site's full survey of the four main views is at /theology/doctrine/last-things.

keyTexts.why: One like a Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus takes this vision as the frame for his own coming in glory.
The LORD comes with his holy ones, his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, and he becomes King over all the earth. The ascension from the same mountain and the promise of return in Acts 1 echo it.
The Lord will suddenly come to his temple, and no one can stand before him unprepared. The prophets saw salvation and judgment in one coming day, which the New Testament finds unfolding in two acts.
No one knows the day or hour, not even the Son. Jesus compares his coming to the flood and to a thief, so the right response is readiness, not calculation.
The Son of Man comes in the clouds and gathers his elect, and the chapter ends with the command to keep watch. It contains the much-debated saying about this generation.
Under oath before the high priest, Jesus joins Psalm 110 and Daniel 7 and claims that his judges will see him enthroned and coming. The claim sealed his condemnation.
Jesus promises to come back and take his friends to be with him. The return is personal: its goal is being where he is.
The same Jesus who ascended will return in the same way. The verse anchors the confession that the return is personal, bodily, and visible.
Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to him at his coming, then the end, when death is destroyed and God is all in all. The return is the hinge between the present reign and the final state.
The dead in Christ rise first, the living are caught up to meet the Lord, and so they will always be with him. Paul writes it to comfort the grieving.
Paul corrects those who thought the day had already come, naming a rebellion and a lawless one who must appear first. The passage restrains both panic and speculation.
Grace has appeared and trains believers to live well while they await the blessed hope, the appearing of their great God and Savior. The two appearings frame the Christian life.
Christ was offered once to bear sins and will appear a second time to bring salvation. The return completes what the cross began rather than adding to it.
Scoffers mock the delay; Peter answers that God's patience is mercy and that the day will come like a thief, bringing a new heaven and a new earth.
The Bible's last promise is Jesus saying he is coming soon, and its last prayer is the church answering, Come, Lord Jesus.

history:
The earliest Christians prayed for the return before they wrote about it. The Aramaic marana tha that Paul leaves untranslated in a Greek letter (1 Corinthians 16:22) shows the prayer was already traditional among Aramaic-speaking believers, and the Didache, a church manual usually dated to the late first or early second century, places it in the prayers after the Lord's Supper (Didache 10) and ends with a chapter urging watchfulness because the Lord will come on the clouds of heaven (Didache 16). Justin Martyr, in the mid-second century, taught plainly that the prophets foretold two comings of Christ, one in humility and suffering and one in glory. The Old Roman baptismal creed that grew into the Apostles' Creed confessed that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, and the Creed of Nicaea (325) said the same. The creed received at Constantinople in 381 added that he will come again in glory and that his kingdom will have no end, a phrase from Luke 1:33 aimed at Marcellus of Ancyra, who taught that Christ's reign would end when he handed the kingdom to the Father.

The early church disagreed about what the return would inaugurate. Papias, Justin, Irenaeus (Against Heresies, book 5, about 180), and Tertullian expected an earthly reign of Christ for a thousand years after he comes, though Justin admitted that many faithful Christians of his day thought otherwise (Dialogue with Trypho 80). The Montanists of the later second century expected the New Jerusalem to descend in Phrygia. Augustine, in book 20 of The City of God (completed about 426), read the thousand years as the present age of the church and refused every attempt to calculate the date, and his reading governed the Western church for a millennium. Medieval hope kept the return vivid in art and liturgy: the Last Judgment over the doors of churches, the sequence Dies Irae (thirteenth century, traditionally attributed to Thomas of Celano), and Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel (1536 to 1541). Joachim of Fiore (died 1202) divided history into three ages and prompted many later speculations about their timing.

The Reformation confessions held to the creed and fenced off speculation. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 17) confesses that Christ will appear to judge and raise the dead, and rejects the teaching that the godly will take possession of the kingdom of the world before the resurrection. The seizure of Münster by radical Anabaptists in 1534 and 1535, who proclaimed it the New Jerusalem, confirmed the reformers' fears. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566, chapter 11) rejects dreams of a golden age on earth before the judgment, and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 33) says God keeps the day unknown so that people will give up carnal security and stay watchful. In the nineteenth century William Miller calculated that Christ would return in 1843 or 1844, and the passing of October 22, 1844, became known as the Great Disappointment; the Seventh-day Adventist Church, organized in 1863, arose from some who reinterpreted it. At the same time John Nelson Darby developed dispensationalism, with a rapture of the church before a future tribulation, spread widely through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909).

Twentieth-century scholarship argued about how near Jesus thought the end was. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, German 1906) held that Jesus expected an immediate end and was wrong; C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) held that the kingdom had fully arrived in Jesus' ministry. Oscar Cullmann (Christ and Time, 1946), Geerhardus Vos, and George Eldon Ladd set out the view most scholars now share, that the kingdom has already come in Christ and is not yet complete until he returns, and Jürgen Moltmann (Theology of Hope, 1964) put the promised future at the center of theology. Through all of it, the churches' shared confession has not moved.

differ.body: The thousand years of Revelation 20 is a symbolic picture of the present age between Christ's two comings, in which Christ reigns from heaven, Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations (Matthew 12:29), and the faithful dead live and reign with Christ. Revelation's visions repeat the same age from different angles rather than marching in one straight line, so chapter 20 does not follow chapter 19 in time. The return is one event, followed at once by one resurrection of the just and the unjust (John 5:28-29), one judgment, and the new creation. Defenders note that Paul moves from Christ's coming straight to the end (1 Corinthians 15:23-24) and that this reading has been held since Augustine by Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed churches alike; modern advocates include Geerhardus Vos and Anthony Hoekema.

Christ returns after a long age in which the gospel, through ordinary preaching and the work of the Spirit, brings the nations broadly under his rule. The parables of the mustard seed and the leaven describe the kingdom growing until it fills the world (Matthew 13:31-33), the Great Commission comes with all authority (Matthew 28:18-20), and Christ must reign until his enemies are subdued (1 Corinthians 15:25). Defenders deny that this is optimism about human nature; it is confidence in the power of God. The view was held by many Puritans, by Jonathan Edwards, and by B. B. Warfield, and it lent confidence to many in the missionary movement of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Christ then returns to a world largely discipled, raises the dead, and judges all.

Christ returns before a thousand-year reign on the earth, and the church passes through the final tribulation rather than being removed from it. Defenders read Revelation 20 in the order it gives: the faithful come to life and reign, and the rest of the dead do not come to life until the thousand years end, and the same verb is used for both groups, so both should be bodily resurrections. They find the same staged order in 1 Corinthians 15:23-24. They note that this was the hope of Papias, Justin, and Irenaeus before Augustine, and they hold one people of God rather than two. George Eldon Ladd gave the view its modern scholarly form.

God's promises to the nation of Israel still stand and will be kept literally. Christ first comes for his church in a rapture (1 Thessalonians 4:17), which most in this tradition place before a seven-year tribulation drawn from the seventieth week of Daniel 9:24-27. During that time God turns again to Israel (Romans 11:25-27). Christ then returns publicly with his saints, reigns from Jerusalem for a thousand years, and after a final rebellion comes the last judgment and the new creation. Defenders argue that this is what consistent reading of prophecy requires and that it honors God's faithfulness to every promise. The system was shaped by John Nelson Darby, spread by C. I. Scofield, and defended by Charles Ryrie and John Walvoord; some in the tradition hold a mid-tribulation or pre-wrath timing of the rapture.

differ.view: Preterist readings of the Olivet Discourse
differ.body: A separate question is how much of Jesus' speech on the Mount of Olives was fulfilled in AD 70. Partial preterists hold that most of Matthew 24 and much of Revelation describe the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and the temple within that generation, using the Old Testament's cosmic language for the fall of cities and empires (Isaiah 13:10), while the bodily return, resurrection, and final judgment remain future. Futurists read much of the same material as describing events just before the final return. Many interpreters hold a mixed reading in which the fall of Jerusalem foreshadows the end. Full preterism, which holds that the return and resurrection already happened in AD 70, is rejected by all these views and by the creeds as denying what the church confesses.

errors:
The church has refused three distortions. The first is denial or dissolution: turning the return into a symbol for moral progress, for the spread of Christ's influence, or for each believer's death, or holding that it already happened in AD 70. Paul called the claim that the resurrection had already taken place a teaching that overturns faith (2 Timothy 2:18), and the creeds confess a coming that is still ahead, personal and public. The second is date-setting and headline-reading. Jesus said the hour is hidden even from the angels (Matthew 24:36) and that it is not for his followers to know the times the Father has fixed (Acts 1:7). Every calculation so far has failed, from the Montanists to William Miller to the paperback charts of the twentieth century, and each has left disillusioned people behind. The New Testament's signs describe the whole age between the comings, not a countdown.

The third distortion is using the return as an escape from the world or as a club. An expectation that the world will be discarded can excuse neglect of creation, of neighbors, and of justice; the New Testament instead connects the return with the renewal of all things (Acts 3:21; Romans 8:21) and with faithful work until the master comes (Matthew 24:45-46). Preaching the return mainly to frighten people into decisions, or to sort Christians by their end-times chart, misuses a hope Paul gave to comfort the grieving (1 Thessalonians 4:18). The church also rejected the opposite errors of the radicals at Münster and others who tried to force the kingdom's arrival by the sword. The kingdom comes when the King comes, and not by human violence.
life:
The return of Christ means the story has an ending, and the ending has a face. Christians do not wait for a cosmic accident or a slow fade into nothing but for a person they know, the one who bore their judgment and now reigns. That shapes grief: Paul does not forbid believers to grieve, but to grieve “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13), because the dead in Christ will rise first. It shapes prayer, since the oldest Christian prayer outside the Lord's Prayer is Maranatha, and every celebration of the Lord's Supper looks ahead “until He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). It shapes the conscience: the one who has this hope purifies himself (1 John 3:3), not out of fear of being caught unready but because he wants to be like the one he will see.

It also gives ordinary work weight. Jesus' parables about his return are almost all about servants doing their jobs faithfully while the master is away. Waiting for Christ does not mean standing on a hill looking at the sky, as the angels told the disciples at the ascension; it means caring for the people and tasks entrusted to you, knowing that the Lord who comes will not let faithful labor be lost (1 Corinthians 15:58). The hidden day keeps a person both steady and alert: steady because the outcome is secure, alert because it could be today.
questions: The prophets saw one great Day of the LORD, but the New Testament finds that day unfolding in two comings of Christ. What does the first coming, in humility, show about what the second will be like?
Jesus says no one knows the day or hour, yet he tells his followers to watch for signs. How do his parables of the servants, the virgins, and the talents define what it means to be ready?
Christians differ over the millennium and the rapture while agreeing that Christ will return in person. Why might the church have put the return in its creeds but left the order of events out?
